paras: The intimidation of John C. Allgood was a hold-up on May 6, 1903, in which armed, masked men stopped Allgood, a Black rural mail carrier, near Gallatin, Sumner County, Tennessee, and told him he would be killed if he kept the job. Postmaster General H. C. Payne suspended the route, and Northern papers likened the case to the Indianola, Mississippi, post office affair. Local whites denied the hold-up had happened, but a federal inspector found that two men had carried it out; Allgood resigned and the route reopened with a new carrier.

Route No. 1 opened on March 1, 1903, and the three highest of five applicants in the civil service examination were Black, leaving the department no choice of appointee. According to the department, the first carrier, Allen F. Dillard, "also colored," resigned within two months, and Allgood, second on the list, was certified on April 26. A Gallatin correspondent of the Baltimore Afro-American wrote instead that Dillard was white and never carried the route, and the Civil Service Commission said Allgood was named after a white man declined. By the correspondent's account, five mail boxes were removed on Allgood's second day and "influential white citizens" circulated petitions for his removal.

Allgood said two masked men stepped from roadside bushes as he opened a gate and told him to resign on reaching Gallatin or be killed. They warned that the next Black man on the route would be killed and that Allgood would be killed if he told. Postmaster H. Swaney wired Washington that the carrier had been "held up by masked men," and that night agent W. F. Conger at Nashville reported that Allgood would not run the route without assurances of safety.

On May 7 Payne suspended the route pending Conger's investigation, saying the only alternatives were to abolish it or send troops, and said he would bring the case to the Attorney General. Within two days a Gallatin special to the Nashville American reported that many citizens, including the county court chairman on whose farm the stop was said to have occurred, disbelieved Allgood, and that four Black farm hands working nearby had seen no strangers.

Conger's report, received about May 20, found that only two men were involved, that the community did not uphold them, and that their identity was uncertain, though Allgood believed he knew them. Payne said there was "not the slightest doubt about the occurrence." Allgood refused to return, fearing for his life, and Payne accepted his resignation and reopened the route, saying patrons should not lose their mail because of "two irresponsible citizens." No report of arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story broke on May 8 through a Washington wire that the New-York Tribune headed "A NEW POSTAL OUTRAGE" and the New York Sun "NEGRO CARRIER TOLD TO QUIT," the Sun citing a departmental wish to punish "kuklux methods." Southern comment turned to doubt and justification: the Montgomery Advertiser suggested the carrier might have been "offensive for other reasons," and the Columbia Herald headed the Gallatin denial "HOLD-UP OF NEGRO CARRIER A FAKE." Representative John Wesley Gaines said rural women feared Black carriers at their doors while the men were in the fields, former governor Benton McMillin agreed, and the Richmond Times-Dispatch backed them in "AN AFFRONT TO THE SOUTH."
Siding with the carrier, the Washington Post, reprinted in Oklahoma, quoted the Memphis Evening Scimitar blaming "a class of whites who rarely write or receive letters."

From May 16 the Black press took up the case; the Afro-American ran its own Gallatin correspondence on the front page, called Allgood "a worthy colored man," and predicted any Black carrier on the route would be "assassinated." The Colored American called Gaines "an odious vulgar liar," and the Wichita Searchlight called the interference "very disgraceful" and urged federal protection for carriers. The Indianapolis Freeman's front page carried what appears to be a cartoon labeled "MR. ALLGOOD," and the Savannah Tribune reported the outcome as "PAYNE DESERTS ALLGOOD," a syndicated item that also ran in the white Bamberg Herald.
Gallatin citizens called the hold-up invented, while the inspector's investigation and Payne affirmed it, the denial coming first and the federal finding later.

reader.title: Intimidation of John C. Allgood
bases: Two (per Allgood and the inspector) armed, masked men stopped a Black rural mail carrier on his route and threatened to kill him if he did not resign; no one was hurt and he gave up the job, not his home (A1, A2, A19, A25).

The hold-up is reported in the officials' telegrams and Allgood's own account (A1, A2, A19), and the federal inspector's investigation led Payne to say there was 'not the slightest doubt' of it (A25, A31), but Gallatin citizens quoted by the Nashville American called it a fabrication (A12, A18).

accounts.label: Officials' telegrams (Washington wire)
accounts.gist: Postmaster Swaney and Inspector Conger reported that the carrier was stopped by armed masked men and his life threatened if he continued; the threat extended to the colored sub-carrier(s).

accounts.label: Allgood's account (Gallatin correspondent)
accounts.gist: Two masked men stepped from bushes as he opened a gate, demanded he resign or be killed, said the next Black carrier would be killed, and that he would be killed if he told.

accounts.label: Gallatin citizens (Nashville American)
accounts.gist: Many residents believed there was no hold-up and that Allgood was afraid; four Black farm hands working nearby said they saw nothing.

accounts.label: Inspector Conger's report
accounts.gist: Only two persons were involved, the community did not uphold them, their identity was uncertain, and the carrier would be safe; Payne said there was no doubt it occurred.

framing.detail: The Washington wire ran as 'A NEW POSTAL OUTRAGE' and 'NEGRO CARRIER TOLD TO QUIT,' likening the case to Indianola and quoting Payne on troops.
Southern papers questioned the story ('HOLD-UP OF NEGRO CARRIER A FAKE') and endorsed Gaines's argument that women feared Black carriers ('AN AFFRONT TO THE SOUTH').
The Washington Post, reprinted in Guthrie, said there was 'no place for the color line' and quoted the Memphis Scimitar blaming a lower class of whites.
The Colored American called Gaines 'an odious vulgar liar'; the Afro-American called Allgood 'a worthy colored man'; the Wichita Searchlight called the interference 'very disgraceful'.
The Savannah Tribune headed the resumption 'PAYNE DESERTS ALLGOOD,' a syndicated item that also ran in the white Bamberg Herald.
